title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 156 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 774–776 (Night 156, continuing directly from nights-155), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 156 continues the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. Abū al-Ḥasan waits at his shop for word from the palace and hears nothing; next morning he finds ʿAlī bedridden, his friends and physicians round him, and ʿAlī, asking only for news of the slave-girl, recites verses of his longing. Back at the shop, the slave-girl at last arrives, troubled, and tells what happened after the lovers parted: Shams al-Nahār lay senseless in the pavilion with the caliph at her side, came to at midnight and blamed something she had eaten; but when the caliph ordered a singing-girl to sing two lines on absent lovers, she fell down in a swoon again. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّادِسَةُ وَالْخَمْسُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sādisatu wa-al-khamsūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the sixth-and-fifty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and fifty-sixth night,
sentences.n: al-sādisa, “the sixth”, is the ordinal, feminine to agree with layla; al-khamsūn, “fifty”, keeps its cardinal form and is joined by wa-.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ أَبَا الْحَسَنِ وَدَّعَهُ فَقَالَ لَهُ عَلِيُّ ابْنُ بَكَّارٍيَا أَخِي لَا تَقْطَعْ عَنِّى الْأَخْبَارَ فَقَالَ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Abā al-Ḥasani waddaʿahu fa-qāla lahu ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin yā akhī lā taqṭaʿ ʿannī al-akhbāra fa-qāla samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Abū al-Ḥasan bade-him-farewell; and ʿAlī son of Bakkār said to-him: O my-brother, do-not cut-off from-me the tidings! And he-said: hearing and obedience.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Abū al-Ḥasan took his leave of ʿAlī, and ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said to him, “My brother, do not leave me without news.” And he answered, “Hearing and obedience.”
sentences.n: The print runs al-saʿīd and anna together (السعيدان); the spacing is kept. In the same way it runs Bakkār into the vocative yā (بكاريا), kept and pointed as one word, Bakkārin yā. Abā al-Ḥasani is accusative after anna (abū becomes abā). Here the print writes ibn with its alif (ابن), where it usually sets بن between two names. lā taqṭaʿ, “do not cut off”: lā with the jussive is a prohibition. The print writes ʿannī, “from me”, with final ى (عنى). samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan, “hearing and obedience”: two accusatives standing for a verb left unsaid, the stock formula of compliance. The shadda of ودّعه is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ أَبَا الْحَسَنِ قَامَ مِنْ عِنْدِهِ وَأَتَى إِلَى دُكَّانِهِ فَفَتَحَهَا وَصَارَ يَرْتَقِبُ خَبَرًا مِنْ عِنْدِ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ فَلَمْ يَأْتِهِ أَحَدٌ بِخَبَرٍ فَبَاتَ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ فِي دَارِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Abā al-Ḥasani qāma min ʿindihi wa-atā ilā dukkānihi fa-fataḥahā wa-ṣāra yartaqibu khabaran min ʿindi Shamsi al-Nahāri fa-lam yaʾtihi aḥadun bi-khabarin fa-bāta tilka al-laylata fī dārihi
sentences.l: Then indeed Abū al-Ḥasan rose from beside-him and came to his-shop and opened-it, and he-began awaiting news from beside Shams al-Nahār; but none came-to-him with news, and he-passed-the-night that night in his-house.
sentences.i: Then Abū al-Ḥasan left him and went to his shop and opened it, and sat waiting for word from Shams al-Nahār; but no one brought him any news, and he spent that night at home.
sentences.n: The print has دارة, a misprint for داره, corrected here. min ʿindihi, “from beside him”: ʿind, “at, with”, is someone's presence or house, and min ʿindi Shamsi al-Nahāri is “from Shams al-Nahār's side”. dukkān, “shop”, takes masculine agreement as a rule, but here the pronoun of fataḥahā, “he opened it”, is feminine: the word is used both ways. ṣāra yartaqibu, “he became awaiting”: ṣāra with an imperfect, “he set about, kept on”. lam yaʾtihi … bi-khabarin, “did not come to him with news”, i.e. did not bring him news: atā bi- is “to bring”, the verb choosing the preposition; after lam the jussive yaʾti has lost the final yāʾ of yaʾtī. bāta, “to spend the night”; tilka al-laylata is an accusative of time. The hamza of يأته and the shadda of دكّانه are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ قَامَ إِلَى أَنْ أَتَى إِلَى دَارِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَدَخَلَ عَلَيْهِ فَوَجَدَهُ مُلْقًي عَلَى فِرَاشِهِ وَأَصْحَابُهُ حَوْلَهُ وَالْحُكَمَاءُ عِنْدَهُ وَكُلُّ وَاحِدٍ يَصِفُ لَهُ شَيْأً وَيَجُسُّونَ يَدَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu qāma ilā an atā ilā dāri ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-dakhala ʿalayhi fa-wajadahu mulqan ʿalā firāshihi wa-aṣḥābuhu ḥawlahu wa-al-ḥukamāʾu ʿindahu wa-kullu wāḥidin yaṣifu lahu shayʾan wa-yajussūna yadahu
sentences.l: And when the morning came-to-morning, he-rose until he came to the house of ʿAlī son of Bakkār and entered upon-him; and he-found-him cast-down on his-bed, and his-companions around-him, and the wise-men with-him, and each one describing for-him a-thing, and they-feel his-hand.
sentences.i: When morning came he rose and made his way to the house of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and went in to him. He found him lying on his bed, his friends about him and the physicians at his side, each prescribing him some remedy while they felt his pulse.
sentences.n: aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu, “the morning dawned”, is a stock phrase of the Nights. qāma ilā an atā, “he rose until he came”: he set out and kept going until he reached the house. dakhala ʿalā, “to go in upon” someone, to visit him in his room. The print writes mulqan, “cast down, lying”, with a final ي (ملقي); a few lines below it spells the same word ملقى. This is the print's usual swapping of ي and ى (as in عنى, “from me”, above), not a different word: the pointing keeps the accusative mulqan, with the tanwīn on the qāf as Classical writes مُلْقًى; read mulqī it would be the active participle, “throwing”. It is accusative, describing ʿAlī's state as he is found. wa-aṣḥābuhu ḥawlahu …, “and his companions around him …”: a string of circumstantial clauses opened by wa-. ḥukamāʾ, “wise men”, here means physicians (ḥakīm, “physician”). yaṣifu lahu shayʾan, “describes for him a thing”, i.e. prescribes him something; li- marks the patient. The print spells shayʾan as شيأ, setting the hamza on the alif of the accusative (Classical شيئا), and that hamza is its own. The verb moves from the singular kullu wāḥidin yaṣifu to the plural yajussūna, “they feel”: the physicians all together. jassa, “to feel with the fingers”; feeling the hand is feeling the pulse. The shadda of يجسّون is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا دَخَلَ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ وَرَآهُ تَبَسَّمَ فَسَلَّمَ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ عَلَيْهِ وَسَأَلَهُ عَنْ حَالِهِ وَجَلَسَ عِنْدَهُ حَتَّى خَرَجَ النَّاسُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā dakhala Abū al-Ḥasani wa-raʾāhu tabassama fa-sallama Abū al-Ḥasani ʿalayhi wa-saʾalahu ʿan ḥālihi wa-jalasa ʿindahu ḥattā kharaja al-nāsu
sentences.l: And when Abū al-Ḥasan entered and he-saw-him, he-smiled; and Abū al-Ḥasan greeted him and asked-him about his-state, and sat with-him until the people went-out.
sentences.i: When Abū al-Ḥasan came in and ʿAlī saw him, he smiled. Abū al-Ḥasan greeted him and asked how he did, and sat with him until the others had gone.
sentences.n: wa-raʾāhu tabassama, “and he saw him, he smiled”: the subjects are not named and shift without warning. The smiler is most likely ʿAlī, glad of the one man who shares his secret, which is why the next clause names Abū al-Ḥasan again; raʾāhu may be ʿAlī seeing his friend come in, or may still be Abū al-Ḥasan, “entered and saw him”. sallama ʿalā, “to greet”, to give someone the salām. The hamzas of رآه and سأله are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ مَا هَذَا الْحَالُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Abū al-Ḥasani mā hādhā al-ḥālu
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan said to-him: What (is) this state?
sentences.i: Then Abū al-Ḥasan said to him, “What state is this?”
sentences.n: ḥāl, “state, condition”, is usually feminine in Classical Arabic (hādhihi al-ḥāl); the print treats it as masculine, hādhā al-ḥāl, as later Arabic often does.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ قَدْ شَاعَ خَبَرِي أَنِّي مَرِيضٌ وَتَسَامَعَ بِذَلِكَ أَصْحَابِي وَلَيْسَ لِي قُوَّةٌ أَسْتَعِينُ بِهَا عَلَى الْقِيَامِ وَالْمَشْيِ حَتَّى أُكَذِّبَ مَنْ جَعَلَنِي ضَعِيفًا وَلَمْ أَزَلْ مُلْقًى مَكَانِي كَمَا تَرَانِي وَقَدْ أَتَتْ أَصْحَابِي إِلَى زِيَارَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin qad shāʿa khabarī annī marīḍun wa-tasāmaʿa bi-dhālika aṣḥābī wa-laysa lī quwwatun astaʿīnu bihā ʿalā al-qiyāmi wa-al-mashyi ḥattā ukadhdhiba man jaʿalanī ḍaʿīfan wa-lam azal mulqan makānī kamā tarānī wa-qad atat aṣḥābī ilā ziyāratī
sentences.l: And ʿAlī son of Bakkār said: My-news has spread, that I (am) sick, and my-companions have-heard-of that one-from-another; and there-is-not to-me strength I-may-seek-help with-it toward the rising and the walking, so-that I-may-give-the-lie-to whoever made-me weak. And I-have-not-ceased cast-down (in) my-place, as you-see-me, and my-companions have-come to my-visiting.
sentences.i: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said, “Word has gone about that I am ill, and all my friends have heard of it. I have no strength to get up and walk about and so give the lie to those who make me out to be weak; I have lain cast down in this one place, as you see me, and my friends have been coming to visit me.”
sentences.n: khabarī annī marīḍun, “my news, that I am sick”: the anna clause spells out what the news is. tasāmaʿa bi-, form VI, “to hear of a thing from one another”, the news passing from mouth to mouth; bi- marks what is heard of. astaʿīnu bihā ʿalā, “by which I may get help toward”: istaʿāna bi- … ʿalā, “to call on something (bi-) for help with something (ʿalā)”. ḥattā ukadhdhiba, “so that I might give the lie to”: ḥattā of purpose with the subjunctive; kadhdhaba (form II) is “to call a liar, prove wrong”, and its shadda is the print's own. man jaʿalanī ḍaʿīfan, “whoever made me weak”, i.e. declared me weak. lam azal, “I have not ceased”, with mulqan, “cast down”, now spelt ملقى as Classical writes it; makānī, “my place”, is an accusative of place. atat aṣḥābī, “my companions have come”: a feminine singular verb with a broken plural of persons, which Classical allows. ilā ziyāratī, “to my visiting”, to visit me.

sentences.t: لَكِنْ يَا أَخِي هَلْ رَأَيْتَ الْجَارِيَةَ أَوْ سَمِعْتَ بِخَبَرٍ مِنْ عِنْدِهَا
sentences.tr: lākin yā akhī hal raʾayta al-jāriyata aw samiʿta bi-khabarin min ʿindihā
sentences.l: But, O my-brother, have you-seen the slave-girl, or heard of news from her-side?
sentences.i: “But tell me, brother, have you seen the slave-girl, or had any word from her?”
sentences.n: lākin, “but”, is the light form, without the shadda of lākinna, and takes no object pronoun. samiʿa bi-, “to hear of”: the verb takes bi- for the thing one gets wind of. min ʿindihā, “from her side”, from her or from those she serves. The hamza of رأيت is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَمْ أَرَهَا مِنْ يَوْمِ فَارَقْتُهَا عَلَى شَاطِئِ الدِّجْلَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lam arahā min yawmi fāraqtuhā ʿalā shāṭiʾi al-Dijlati
sentences.l: And he-said: I-have-not seen-her since the day I-parted-from-her on the bank of the Tigris.
sentences.i: He said, “I have not seen her since the day I left her on the bank of the Tigris.”
sentences.n: lam arahā, “I have not seen her”: ara is the jussive of raʾā after lam, which has lost both its hamza and its final letter. min yawmi fāraqtuhā, “from the day I parted from her”: yawm is annexed straight to a verbal clause, with no word for “when”. The print gives the river the article, al-Dijla, where Classical Arabic says Dijla without it. The hamza of شاطئ is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ يَا أَخِي احْذَرِ الْفَضِيحَةَ وَاتْرُكْ هَذَا الْبُكَاءَ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla lahu Abū al-Ḥasani yā akhī iḥdhari al-faḍīḥata wa-utruk hādhā al-bukāʾa
sentences.l: Then Abū al-Ḥasan said to-him: O my-brother, beware-of the scandal, and leave this weeping.
sentences.i: Then Abū al-Ḥasan said to him, “My brother, beware of scandal, and give over this weeping.”
sentences.n: iḥdhari al-faḍīḥata, “beware of the scandal”: the imperative iḥdhar takes a helping -i before the article. faḍīḥa is public disgrace, the exposure of what should stay hidden, and an affair with the caliph's favourite is exactly what must not come out.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍيَا أَخِي لَا أَمْلِكُ نَفْسِي ثُمَّ أَنْشَدَ وَجَعَلَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin yā akhī lā amliku nafsī thumma anshada wa-jaʿala yaqūlu
sentences.l: And ʿAlī son of Bakkār said: O my-brother, I-do-not possess my-self. Then he-recited and began saying:
sentences.i: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār answered, “My brother, I am not master of myself.” Then he began to recite:
sentences.n: Again the print runs Bakkār into yā (بكاريا); the spacing is kept. lā amliku nafsī, “I do not own myself”: I cannot control myself, as was said of him in the last night. jaʿala yaqūlu, “he set about saying”: jaʿala with an imperfect means “to begin to”.

sentences.t:
نَارَتْ عَلَى يَدِهَا مَا لَمْ تَنَلْهُ يَدِي * نَقَشْ عَلَى مِعْصَمٍ اَوْهَتْ بِهِ جَلَدِي
خَافَتْ عَلَى يَدِهَا مِنْ نَبْلِ مُقْلَتِهَا * فَاَلْبَسَتْ يَدَهَا دِرْعًا مِنَ الزَّرَدِ
جَسَّ الطَّبِيبُ يَدِي جَهْلًا فَقُلْتُ لَهُ * اِنَّ التَّأَلُّمَ فِي قَلْبِي فَخَلِّ يَدِي
قَالَتْ لِطَيْفِ خَيَالٍ زَارَنِي وَمَضَى * بِاللّٰهِ صِفْهُ وَلَا تَنْقُصْ وَلَا تَزِدِ
فَقَالَ خَلَّفْتُهُ لَوْ مَاتَ مِنْ ظَمَأٍ * وَقُلْتُ قِفْ عَنْ وُرُودِ الْمَاءِ لَمْ يَرِدِ
فَاسْتَمْطَرَتْ لُؤْلُؤًا مِنْ نَرْجِسٍ وَسَقَتْ * وَرْدًا وَعَضَّتْ عَلَى الْعُنَّابِ بِالْبَرَدِ
sentences.tr:
nārat ʿalā yadihā mā lam tanalhu yadī * naqash ʿalā miʿṣamin awhat bihi jaladī
khāfat ʿalā yadihā min nabli muqlatihā * fa-albasat yadahā dirʿan mina al-zaradi
jassa al-ṭabību yadī jahlan fa-qultu lahu * inna al-taʾalluma fī qalbī fa-khalli yadī
qālat li-ṭayfi khayālin zāranī wa-maḍā * bi-Allāhi ṣifhu wa-lā tanquṣ wa-lā tazidi
fa-qāla khallaftuhu law māta min ẓamaʾin * wa-qultu qif ʿan wurūdi al-māʾi lam yaridi
fa-istamṭarat luʾluʾan min narjisin wa-saqat * wardan wa-ʿaḍḍat ʿalā al-ʿunnābi bi-al-baradi
sentences.l:
There-shone upon her-hand what my-hand has-not attained: * tracery upon a wrist, with-which she-has-worn-down my-endurance;
she-feared for her-hand from the arrows of her-eye, * so she-clothed her-hand (in) a coat-of-mail of chain-rings.
The physician felt my-hand in-ignorance, so I-said to-him: * Indeed the aching (is) in my-heart, so let-go my-hand.
She-said to-a-phantom of-a-vision (that) visited-me and went-on: * By God, describe-him, and do-not take-away and do-not add.
And it-said: I-left-him (such that) if he-were-dying of thirst * and I-said, Hold-back from coming-down-to the water, he-would-not come-down.
Then she-drew-down-rain of pearls from narcissus and watered * rose, and bit upon the jujube with the hail.
sentences.i:
Upon her hand there shines what my own hand has never won: a tracery on her wrist that has worn my endurance away.
She feared for her hand from the arrows of her own eyes, and so she clad it in a coat of chain-mail.
The physician, not knowing, took me by the hand; I told him, “The pain is in my heart, so let my hand go.”
She said to the phantom that visited me by night and went its way, “By God, describe him to me, and take nothing away and add nothing.”
It said, “I left him so that, were he dying of thirst and I told him to keep from the water, he would not go down to it.”
Then she drew down a rain of pearls from narcissus and watered roses, and bit upon jujubes with hail.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of اَوْهَتْ, فَاَلْبَسَتْ and اِنَّ, where the edition marks no hamza; the hamzas of التَّأَلُّمَ, ظَمَأٍ and لُؤْلُؤًا and the dagger alif of بِاللّٰهِ are the print's too. The metre is basīṭ, rhyming in -dī. The poem is on the beloved's hennaed hand. Line 1 is doubtful at both ends of its first half. The print has نَارَتْ, nārat, “(there) shone”, which gives a strained sense; the parallel with tanalhu, “(my hand) has not attained”, strongly suggests nālat, “she has gained (on her hand)”, with ل misread as ر, but the reading is kept since nārat can just be construed. The print points the next word نَقَشْ, which does not scan; the sense and metre want the noun naqsh, “tracery”, the henna pattern on her wrist, most likely naqshan, explaining the mā before it. awhat bihi jaladī, “she has weakened my fortitude with it”: awhā, form IV, “to make frail”. In line 2 nabl, “arrows”, are her own glances, and the coat of chain-mail is the henna's ring pattern. In line 3 the physician takes the lover's hand to feel the pulse, and jahlan, “in ignorance”, is accusative of manner; khalli is the imperative of khallā, “to let go”. In line 4 the speaker shifts: she, the beloved, asks the ṭayf al-khayāl, the phantom that brings a lover's image by night, about him; ṣifhu, “describe him”, is the imperative of waṣafa with -hu; tanquṣ and tazid are jussives after lā of prohibition, the final kasra of tazidi supplied for the rhyme, as with yaridi below. Line 5: law māta, “even if he were dying”, with lam yarid, “he would not come down (to drink)”, as the answer: he is so obedient to her that he would die of thirst at a word. Line 6 is a set piece: pearls are tears, narcissus eyes, roses cheeks, jujubes her reddened fingertips, and hail her teeth; istamṭara, form X, “to seek rain from”; ʿaḍḍa ʿalā, “to bite on”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ قَالَ يَا أَبَا الْحَسَنِ قَدْ بُلِيتُ بِمُصِيبَةٍ كُنْتُ فِي أَمْنٍ مِنْهَا وَلَيْسَ لِي أَعْظَمُ رَاحَةٍ مِنَ الْمَوْتِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi qāla yā Abā al-Ḥasani qad bulītu bi-muṣībatin kuntu fī amnin minhā wa-laysa lī aʿẓamu rāḥatin mina al-mawti
sentences.l: And when he-finished from his-poetry, he-said: O Abū al-Ḥasan, I-have-been-afflicted with a-calamity (that) I-was in safety from-it, and there-is-not for-me a-greater relief than death.
sentences.i: When he had finished his verses, he said, “Abū al-Ḥasan, a calamity has fallen on me that I never thought could touch me, and no relief is left to me greater than death.”
sentences.n: faragha min, “to be done with”. qad bulītu bi-, “I have been afflicted with”: the passive of balā, “to try, afflict”, with bi- naming the affliction; the damma of بليتُ is the print's own. kuntu fī amnin minhā, “I was in safety from it”, describes muṣība with no relative word, as Arabic does after an indefinite noun: a calamity he had thought himself safe from. laysa lī aʿẓamu rāḥatin mina al-mawti, “there is not for me a greater relief than death”: li- marks the one who has or lacks a thing, and the elative aʿẓam with min is comparative. After yā, abā is accusative because it heads a construct.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ اصْبِرْ لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ يَشْفِيكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Abū al-Ḥasani iṣbir laʿalla Allāha yashfīka
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan said to-him: Be-patient; perhaps God will-heal-you.
sentences.i: “Be patient,” Abū al-Ḥasan told him; “it may be that God will heal you.”
sentences.n: laʿalla, “perhaps”, voices a hope and, like inna, puts its subject in the accusative (Allāha). yashfīka, from shafā, “to heal”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَزَلَ أَبُو الْحَسَنِ مِنْ عِنْدِهِ وَجَاءَ إِلَى دُكَّانِهِ وَفَتَحَهَا
sentences.tr: thumma nazala Abū al-Ḥasani min ʿindihi wa-jāʾa ilā dukkānihi wa-fataḥahā
sentences.l: Then Abū al-Ḥasan went-down from his-presence and came to his-shop and opened-it.
sentences.i: Then Abū al-Ḥasan left him and went to his shop and opened it.
sentences.n: nazala min ʿindihi, “he came down from his presence”: the sick man lay in an upper room, and to leave him is to come down. dukkān, “shop”, is treated here as feminine (fataḥahā, “opened it”, with -hā); the word is used in either gender. The shadda of دكّانه is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَمَا جَلَسَ غَيْرَ قَلِيلٍ وَإِذَا بِالْجَارِيَةِ أَقْبَلَتْ إِلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَتْ عَلَيْهِ فَرَدَّ عَلَيْهَا السَّلَامَ
sentences.tr: fa-mā jalasa ghayra qalīlin wa-idhā bi-al-jāriyati aqbalat ilayhi wa-sallamat ʿalayhi fa-radda ʿalayhā al-salāma
sentences.l: And he-had-not sat other-than a-little, and behold, the slave-girl came-toward-him and greeted-him, and he-returned to-her the greeting.
sentences.i: He had sat there only a little while when, all at once, the slave-girl came up to him and greeted him, and he returned her greeting.
sentences.n: mā jalasa ghayra qalīlin, “he did not sit other than a little”, that is, he had sat only a short while: ghayra is accusative, standing where the adverb would. wa-idhā bi-al-jāriyati, “and behold, the slave-girl”: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears, and aqbalat, “she came toward”, follows as a fresh verb. sallama ʿalā, “to greet”; radda ʿalayhā al-salāma, “he returned the greeting to her”.

sentences.t: وَنَظَرَ إِلَيْهَا فَوَجَدَهَا خَافِقَةَ الْقَلْبِ مَهْمُومَةً يَظْهَرُ عَلَيْهَا أَثَرُ الْكَأْبَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-naẓara ilayhā fa-wajadahā khāfiqata al-qalbi mahmūmatan yaẓharu ʿalayhā atharu al-kaʾbati
sentences.l: And he-looked at-her and found-her throbbing of-heart, care-laden, there-appearing upon-her the trace of the dejection.
sentences.i: Looking at her, he saw that her heart was fluttering and she was weighed down with care, and the marks of sorrow showed on her.
sentences.n: The print has حافقة, a misprint for خافقة, corrected here. khāfiqata al-qalbi, “throbbing of heart”: an adjective governing a noun, with her heart doing the throbbing. wajada, “to find”, takes its object and then what it was found to be, so khāfiqata and mahmūmatan, “care-laden”, are both accusative. yaẓharu ʿalayhā …, “there appears upon her …”, is a circumstantial clause without wa-. The print spells the last word الكأبة, with the hamza on an alif and no long ā after it; it is read kaʾba, a form recorded beside the usual kaʾāba, “gloom, dejection”. The hamza is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا كَيْفَ حَالُ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā ahlan wa-sahlan kayfa ḥālu Shamsi al-Nahāri
sentences.l: And he-said to-her: Family and level-ground! How (is) the state of Shams al-Nahār?
sentences.i: He said to her, “Welcome, welcome! How is Shams al-Nahār?”
sentences.n: ahlan wa-sahlan, the old welcome: “(you have come to) family, and (you tread) level ground”, both accusative after an unspoken verb. kayfa ḥālu …, “how is the state of …”, simply “how is she?”

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ سَوْفَ أُخْبِرُكَ عَنْ حَالِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat sawfa ukhbiruka ʿan ḥālihā
sentences.l: And she-said: I-shall inform-you about her-state.
sentences.i: “I shall tell you how she is,” she said.
sentences.n: sawfa marks the future. akhbara, form IV, “to inform”, takes the person told as its object and ʿan for the matter told about.

sentences.t: كَيْفَ حَالُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: kayfa ḥālu ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin
sentences.l: How (is) the state of ʿAlī son of Bakkār?
sentences.i: “How is ʿAlī ibn Bakkār?”
sentences.n: kayfa ḥālu, “how is the state of”, the usual way to ask after someone: a sentence with no verb, in which kayfa, “how”, is the predicate placed first and ḥāl the subject.

sentences.t: فَأَخْبَرَهَا أَبُو الْحَسَنِ بِجَمِيعِ مَا كَانَ وَبِمَا تَمَّ مِنْ أَمْرِهِ فَتَأَسَّفَتْ وَتَوَجَّعَتْ وَتَأَوَّهَتْ وَتَعَجَّبَتْ مِنْ هَذَا الْأَمْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhbarahā Abū al-Ḥasani bi-jamīʿi mā kāna wa-bi-mā tamma min amrihi fa-taʾassafat wa-tawajjaʿat wa-taʾawwahat wa-taʿajjabat min hādhā al-amri
sentences.l: And Abū al-Ḥasan informed-her of all that had-been, and of what was-completed of his-affair; and she-grieved and felt-pain and sighed-“ah” and marvelled at this matter.
sentences.i: Abū al-Ḥasan told her all that had happened and how things had gone with ʿAlī; and she grieved and was pained, she sighed and marvelled at it all.
sentences.n: akhbara … bi-, “to inform someone of”: the verb takes the person as its object and the news with bi-, here twice (bi-jamīʿi, wa-bi-mā). min amrihi, “of his affair”, is ʿAlī's. The four verbs are all form V, taʾassafa, tawajjaʿa, taʾawwaha, taʿajjaba, and chime with one another: “she grieved, ached, sighed, wondered”; taʾawwaha is to say āh, “ah!”. The hamza of فتأسفت and تأوّهت and the shaddas of تمّ, توجّعت and تأوّهت are the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ إِنَّ سَيِّدَتِي حَالُهَا أَعْجَبُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat inna sayyidatī ḥāluhā aʿjabu min dhālika
sentences.l: Then she-said: Indeed my-lady, her-state (is) more-wondrous than that.
sentences.i: Then she said, “My lady's case is stranger still.
sentences.n: inna sayyidatī ḥāluhā aʿjabu, “indeed my lady — her state is more wondrous”: the topic sayyidatī stands first, accusative after inna (its -a hidden under the possessive -ī), and a whole sentence, ḥāluhā aʿjabu, is its predicate, the -hā pointing back to her. aʿjab is the elative of ʿajīb, “wondrous”, with min, “than”.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّكُمْ لَمَّا مَضَيْتُمْ وَتَوَجَّهْتُمْ رَجَعْتُ وَقَلْبِي يَخْفِقُ عَلَيْكُمْ وَمَا صَدَّقْتُ بِنَجَاتِكُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-innakum lammā maḍaytum wa-tawajjahtum rajaʿtu wa-qalbī yakhfiqu ʿalaykum wa-mā ṣaddaqtu bi-najātikum
sentences.l: For indeed you — when you-went-off and turned-your-faces (away), I-went-back, my-heart throbbing over-you, and I-did-not believe in your-safe-escape.
sentences.i: For when you had gone off on your way, I turned back with my heart pounding for you, scarcely believing that you had got away safe.
sentences.n: fa-innakum, “for indeed you”: the sentence begins with inna and the pronoun -kum, then changes course, and the lammā clause takes over with a new subject, “I”; a loose construction of speech. The plural “you” takes in both men. wa-qalbī yakhfiqu, “my heart throbbing”, is a circumstantial clause; khafaqa ʿalā, “to beat (in fear) for”. ṣaddaqa bi-, “to believe in”: bi- marks what is believed. The shaddas of فانّكم and توجّهتم are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَجَعْتُ وَجَدْتُ سَيِّدَتِي مَطْرُوحَةً فِى الْقُبَّةِ لَا تَتَكَلَّمُ وَلَا تَرُدُّ جَوَابًا عَلَى أَحَدٍ وَأَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ جَالِسٌ عِنْدَ رَأْسِهَا لَا يَجِدُ مَنْ يُخْبِرُهُ بِخَبَرِهَا وَلَا يَعْلَمُ مَا بِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā rajaʿtu wajadtu sayyidatī maṭrūḥatan fī al-qubbati lā tatakallamu wa-lā taruddu jawāban ʿalā aḥadin wa-amīru al-muʾminīna jālisun ʿinda raʾsihā lā yajidu man yukhbiruhu bi-khabarihā wa-lā yaʿlamu mā bihā
sentences.l: And when I-returned, I-found my-lady cast-down in the domed-hall, not speaking and not returning an-answer to anyone, and the Commander of the Faithful sitting at her-head, not finding who might-inform-him of her-news, and not knowing what (is) with-her.
sentences.i: When I got back I found my lady lying prostrate in the pavilion, speaking not a word and answering no one, and the Commander of the Faithful sitting at her head, with no one to tell him what had befallen her, and no notion what ailed her.
sentences.n: maṭrūḥatan, “thrown down”, is accusative, describing her as she was found. al-qubba, “the dome”, is the domed hall of the palace where the caliph sits. radda jawāban ʿalā, “to return an answer to”. wa-amīru al-muʾminīna jālisun, “while the Commander of the Faithful was sitting”, is a circumstantial clause. akhbara … bi-, “to inform of”: bi- marks the news. mā bihā, “what is in her”, what ails her: bi- of place. The damma on the final tāʾ of رجعتُ and وجدتُ is the print's own, marking “I”; so are the shadda of تتكلّم and the hamza of المؤمنين and رأسها. The print writes fī as فى.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ تَزَلْ فِي غَشْيَتِهَا إِلَى نِصْفِ اللَّيْلِ ثُمَّ أَفَاقَتْ
sentences.tr: wa-lam tazal fī ghashyatihā ilā niṣfi al-layli thumma afāqat
sentences.l: And she-did-not cease in her-swoon until the half of the night; then she-came-to.
sentences.i: She lay in her swoon until midnight, and then came to herself.
sentences.n: lam tazal fī, “she did not cease (being) in”: she stayed. niṣf al-layl, “the half of the night”, is midnight.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ مَا الَّذِي أَصَابَكِ يَا شَمْسَ النَّهَارِ وَمَا الَّذِي اعْتَرَاكِ فِي هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā amīru al-muʾminīna mā alladhī aṣābaki yā Shamsa al-Nahāri wa-mā alladhī iʿtarāki fī hādhihi al-laylati
sentences.l: And the Commander of the Faithful said to-her: What (is) that-which struck-you, O Shams al-Nahār, and what (is) that-which came-upon-you in this night?
sentences.i: The Commander of the Faithful said to her, ‘What has befallen you, Shams al-Nahār, and what has come over you tonight?’
sentences.n: mā alladhī, “what is it that”, a question built on a relative clause. aṣāba, “to strike, befall”, and iʿtarā, form VIII of ʿarā, “to come upon, seize” (of illness or care); -ki is the feminine “you”. After yā the name Shams al-Nahār, “Sun of the Day”, is accusative, Shamsa, because its first word governs the second.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ كَلَامَ الْخَلِيفَةِ قَبَّلَتْ أَقْدَامَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat Shamsu al-Nahāri kalāma al-khalīfati qabbalat aqdāmahu
sentences.l: And when Shams al-Nahār heard the words of the caliph, she-kissed his-feet,
sentences.i: When Shams al-Nahār heard the caliph speak, she kissed his feet
sentences.n: qabbala, form II, “to kiss”. aqdām, the plural of qadam, “foot”, stands where Classical usage would have the dual, qadamayhi, as often in later prose.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ جَعَلَنِى اللَّهُ فِدَاكَ إِنَّهُ خَامَرَنِي خِلْطٌ فَأَضْرَمَ النَّارَ فِي جَسَدِى وَغُشِيَ عَلَيَّ مِنْ شِدَّةِ مَابِي وَلَا أَعْلَمُ كَيْفَ كَانَ حَالِي
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahu yā amīra al-muʾminīna jaʿalanī Allāhu fidāka innahu khāmaranī khilṭun fa-aḍrama al-nāra fī jasadī wa-ghushiya ʿalayya min shiddati mā bī wa-lā aʿlamu kayfa kāna ḥālī
sentences.l: and said to-him: O Commander of the Faithful, may God make-me your-ransom! Indeed (it is that) a humour pervaded-me and kindled the fire in my-body, and it-was-swooned upon-me from the intensity of what (was) in-me, and I-do-not know how my-state was.
sentences.i: and said to him, ‘O Commander of the Faithful, may God make me your ransom! A humour rose in me and lit a fire through my body, and I swooned for the violence of it, and I know nothing of what became of me.’
sentences.n: jaʿalanī Allāhu fidāka, “may God make me your ransom”, a courteous formula of devotion: the perfect jaʿala here expresses a wish. innahu, “indeed it (is that)”: the -hu is the pronoun of the matter, pointing ahead to the whole clause. khilṭ is one of the four humours of the old medicine (blood, phlegm, yellow and black bile), whose excess brings on fever; khāmara, “to pervade, take hold of”, as wine takes hold of the mind. ghushiya ʿalayya, “there was a swooning upon me”, the impersonal passive of ghashiya: “I fainted”. The print runs mā bī, “what was in me”, together (مابي); it is kept and pointed as one word. The print writes the final ي of jaʿalanī and jasadī as ى; the shadda of عليّ is its own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا الْخَلِيفَةُ مَا الَّذِي اسْتَعْمَلْتِهِ فِي نَهَارِكِ فَقَالَتْ أَفْطَرْتُ عَلَى شَيْءٍ لَمْ آكُلْهُ قَطُّ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-khalīfatu mā alladhī istaʿmaltihi fī nahāriki fa-qālat afṭartu ʿalā shayʾin lam ākulhu qaṭṭu
sentences.l: And the caliph said to-her: What (is) that-which you-took in your-day? And she-said: I-broke-fast on a-thing I-did-not eat-it ever.
sentences.i: The caliph asked her, ‘What have you taken today?’ and she said, ‘I broke my fast on something I had never eaten before.’
sentences.n: istaʿmala, “to use”, here “to take” food or medicine; istaʿmaltihi is “you (f.) took it”, the -i- of the feminine showing before the object -hi. afṭara ʿalā, “to break one's fast on”: ʿalā marks the first food of the day. lam ākulhu qaṭṭu, “I never ate it”: lam with the jussive ākul, and qaṭṭu, “ever”, which goes only with a negated past. The hamza of آكله and the shadda of قطّ are the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا أَظْهَرَتِ الْقُوَّةَ وَاسْتَدْعَتْ بِشَيْءٍ مِنَ الشَّرَابِ فَشَرِبَتْهُ ثُمَّ سَأَلَتِ الْمَلِكَ أَنْ يَعُودَ إِلَى انْشِرَاحِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā aẓharati al-quwwata wa-istadʿat bi-shayʾin mina al-sharābi fa-sharibathu thumma saʾalati al-malika an yaʿūda ilā inshirāḥihi
sentences.l: Then indeed she showed the strength, and called for something of the drink, and drank-it; then she-asked the king that he-return to his-good-cheer.
sentences.i: Then she made a show of strength, called for something to drink and drank it, and begged the king to go back to his merrymaking.
sentences.n: aẓharat al-quwwata, “she showed strength”: she put on a brave face. istadʿā bi-, “to call for”: bi- marks what is sent for. sharāb, “drink”, is often wine in the Nights. inshirāḥ, “expansion (of the breast)”, is good cheer, here the evening's entertainment that her collapse had broken off; an yaʿūda, “that he return”, subjunctive after an. Hārūn is called al-malik, “the king”, as well as caliph. The hamza of سألت is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسَ الْمَلِكُ عَلَى سَرِيرِهِ فِى الْقُبَّةِ وَالْمَجْلِسُ مُنْتَظِمٌ
sentences.tr: fa-jalasa al-maliku ʿalā sarīrihi fī al-qubbati wa-al-majlisu muntaẓimun
sentences.l: So the king sat on his-couch in the domed-hall, and the gathering (was) in-order.
sentences.i: So the king took his seat on his couch in the pavilion, and the company was set in order once more.
sentences.n: sarīr, a raised couch or throne. wa-al-majlisu muntaẓimun, “the gathering in order”, is a circumstantial clause; muntaẓim is the form VIII participle of naẓama, “to string (pearls)”, so “set in order”. The print writes fī as فى.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جِئْتُ إِلَيْهَا سَأَلَتْنِي عَنْ حَالِكُمَا فَأَخْبَرْتُهَا بِمَا فَعَلْتُ مَعَكُمَا وَأَنْشَدْتُهَا مَا قَالَهُ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ فِى الْوَدَاعِ فَبَكَتْ سِرًّا ثُمَّ سَكَتَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā jiʾtu ilayhā saʾalatnī ʿan ḥālikumā fa-akhbartuhā bi-mā faʿaltu maʿakumā wa-anshadtuhā mā qālahu ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin fī al-wadāʿi fa-bakat sirran thumma sakatat
sentences.l: And when I-came to-her, she-asked-me about the state of-you-two, and I-informed-her of what I-did with-you-two, and I-recited-to-her what ʿAlī son of Bakkār said at the farewell; and she-wept secretly, then fell-silent.
sentences.i: When I came to her she asked me how you both were, and I told her what I had done with you, and recited to her the verses ʿAlī ibn Bakkār spoke at parting; and she wept in secret, and then fell silent.
sentences.n: ḥālikumā, “the state of you two”: the dual -kumā, Abū al-Ḥasan and ʿAlī. akhbara … bi-mā, “told her of what”: bi- marks the news. anshada, “to recite (verse)”, takes two objects, the hearer -hā and the poem, mā qālahu, “what he said”. sirran, “in secret”, is an accusative used as an adverb. The hamza of جئت and سألتني and the shadda of سرّا are the print's own; the print writes fī as فى.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ جَلَسَ وَأَمَرَ جَارِيَةً أَنْ تُغَنِّيَ فَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna amīra al-muʾminīna jalasa wa-amara jāriyatan an tughanniya fa-anshadat taqūlu
sentences.l: Then indeed the Commander of the Faithful sat and ordered a slave-girl that she-sing; and she-recited, saying:
sentences.i: Then the Commander of the Faithful sat down and ordered a slave-girl to sing, and she sang:
sentences.n: After inna the title takes the accusative, amīra. amara … an tughanniya, “ordered … that she sing”: subjunctive after an. anshadat taqūlu, “she recited, saying”: the imperfect taqūlu goes with the verb of reciting, the usual way the Nights brings on verse.

sentences.t:
لَعَمْرِي لَا يَحْلُو لِيَ الْعَيْشُ بَعْدَكُمْ * فَيَا لَيْتَ شِعْرِي كَيْفَ حَالُكُمْ بَعْدِي
يَحِقُّ لِلدَمْعِي اَنْ يَكُونَ مِنَ الدِّمَا * اِذَا كُنْتُمْ تَبْكُونَ دَمْعًا عَلَى بُعْدِي
sentences.tr:
la-ʿamrī lā yaḥlū liya al-ʿayshu baʿdakum * fa-yā layta shiʿrī kayfa ḥālukum baʿdī
yaḥiqqu li-al-damʿī an yakūna mina al-dimā * idhā kuntum tabkūna damʿan ʿalā buʿdī
sentences.l:
By-my-life, life is-not-sweet to-me after-you; * so O would-that my-knowing — how (is) your-state after-me?
It-is-right for the-my-tears that it-be of blood, * when you are-weeping tears over my-distance.
sentences.i:
By my life, there is no sweetness in living now that you are gone; would that I knew how you fare without me!
Well may my tears be tears of blood, when you yourselves are weeping tears that I am far away.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of اَنْ and اِذَا, where the edition marks no hamza. la-ʿamrī, “by my life”, is an oath. yā layta shiʿrī, “O would that my knowing”, is the fixed phrase “would that I knew”, followed by the question it longs to have answered. al-dimā, “blood”, is the plural dimāʾ with its final hamza dropped, as verse allows. The second line turns on the comparison: if you shed mere tears for my absence, it is only right that mine should be blood. The print's لِلدَمْعِي is doubtful: it sets the article and the possessive “my” on one noun, which Arabic does not do, and the dāl has a plain fatḥa with no shadda, where the article (lid-damʿ) would need one; the likeliest reading is لِدَمْعِي, li-damʿī, “for my tears”, with one lām set twice. It is kept as printed and translated by that sense.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ سَيِّدَتِي هَذَا الشِّعْرَ وَقَعَتْ عَلَى الصُّفَّةِ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat sayyidatī hādhā al-shiʿra waqaʿat ʿalā al-ṣuffati maghshiyyan ʿalayhā
sentences.l: And when my-lady heard this poetry, she-fell on the bench, swooned-upon.
sentences.i: When my lady heard these verses, she fell down upon the dais in a swoon.
sentences.n: al-ṣuffa is a raised bench or dais along the wall of a room (the word behind English “sofa”); the print's الصفة could also be read al-ṣifa, “the quality, manner”, but that gives no sense here. maghshiyyan ʿalayhā, “swooned upon”: the passive participle stays masculine even of a woman, because it agrees with the impersonal swoon, and ʿalayhā names the one it came over; it is accusative, describing her state.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she ceased the speech allowed her.
